terms.definition: training a program (an agent) by letting it act and giving it rewards, instead of showing it the right answer.
the program that observes, chooses actions and collects rewards.
everything the agent acts on: it receives the action and sends back an observation and a reward.
what the agent can see of the current situation, e.g. CartPole's 4 numbers.
what the agent does at one step, e.g. push the cart left (0) or right (1).
the number the environment sends back after each action: positive = good, negative = bad.
the device that switches heating or cooling on and off to keep a room at a set temperature.
Google's AI research lab.
1970s–80s video games, used as a standard test for game-playing agents.
machine learning with neural networks of many layers.
a model built from many small parts (neurons) arranged in layers; each part does a little arithmetic and passes its result on.
one small part of a neural network: a weighted sum of its inputs passed through a fixed curve.
a group of neurons working side by side; a network is several layers, each feeding the next.
a number the network learns; each input is multiplied by its weight.
working out which of many earlier actions deserves the credit or blame for a reward that came later.
one complete run, from reset until the task ends (the pole falls) or a step limit is hit.
the rule the agent uses to choose an action from an observation.
any method that tries many policies and keeps the ones that collect more reward.
the few numbers that define a policy; the policy space is every possible combination of them.
involving chance: the same situation can lead to different actions or outcomes.
trying every combination (or a great many) and keeping the best.
keep a population of policies, drop the worst, and make copies of the best with small random changes, generation after generation.
adjusting the policy's parameters in the direction that increases the reward (using gradients).
for one parameter: how much and in which direction a result changes when the parameter is nudged.
a Python library of simulated environments with one standard interface (reset and step); gymnasium is its maintained successor.
software that imitates a real system, so an agent can practise without real hardware.
the simulated task of keeping a pole balanced on a cart by pushing the cart left or right.
reset() starts an episode and returns the first observation; step(action) does the action and returns what happened.
the list of actions an environment accepts, e.g. Discrete(2) = the integers 0 and 1.
the two ways an episode stops: done = it really ended (the pole fell), truncated = it was cut off by a step limit.
the score of a simple method that any learned one must beat; here the hand-written policy's 41.7 steps.
the S-shaped curve that turns any number into one between 0 and 1.
the fixed curve applied to a neuron's sum.
turns a row of scores into probabilities that add up to 1.
the trade-off between trying actions to learn more (exploring) and using the best one known so far (exploiting).
a layer between the input and the output.
the activation max(0, x).
the part of Google's TensorFlow library used to build and train neural networks.
Google's library for neural networks; code calls it tf.
an ordinary layer where every input feeds every neuron.
in Keras, fix a model's loss and optimizer before training.
the one number that says how wrong the outputs are; training changes the weights to make it smaller.
an action that is a dial setting, like a steering angle, not one of a short list.
sparse = most steps pay nothing; delayed = the reward comes long after the action that earned it.
an action's discounted sum of all the rewards that came after it.
γ (gamma), between 0 and 1: how much a reward one step later counts, compared with one now.
how much better (positive) or worse (negative) an action's return was than the average return.
the basic policy-gradient algorithm: play episodes, then make each action more (or less) likely according to its advantage.
TensorFlow's recorder: it remembers the calculations done inside it so their gradients can be computed.
the algorithm that changes the weights using gradients, e.g. Nadam.
Adam is a popular optimizer that adapts each weight's step size; Nadam is a small improvement of it.
the usual loss for a yes/no prediction; used here to compute the gradient that makes the chosen action more likely.
needing a very large number of episodes of practice before it improves.
the learnable numbers of a model: its weights and biases.
stochastic gradient descent: nudging the weights after every small batch (here, after every sample).
the training method: again and again, nudge every weight a little in the direction that lowers the loss.
states that change at random from step to step, where the next state depends only on the current one.
a Markov chain where an agent chooses an action at each state, and actions give rewards.
the situation the agent is in, e.g. s0, s1 or s2 in Figure 18-8.
T(s, a, s′): the chance that action a in state s lands in state s′.
the value of a state = the reward of the best action plus the discounted value of where it leads, on average.
V*(s): the discounted rewards the agent can expect from state s if it acts as well as possible.
Q(s, a): the discounted rewards the agent can expect after doing action a in state s, then acting as well as possible.
computing state values by starting at 0 and applying the Bellman equation over and over.
solving a problem by reusing the answers to smaller versions of it, round after round.
the position of the largest value: here, which action has the highest Q-value.
the average result, each outcome weighted by its probability.
updating a value estimate after every single step, towards (reward + discounted value of the next state).
α (alpha): what fraction of the way an estimate moves towards the new evidence.
the rule used to move around while learning, often completely random.
updating one estimate using another estimate.
learning Q-values from experience alone, by TD updates, without knowing the transition probabilities.
off-policy = learns about one policy (the best) while acting with another (e.g. random); on-policy = learns about the policy it is acting with.
act randomly with probability ε (epsilon), otherwise take the action with the highest Q-value.
always take the action with the highest current estimate.
a bonus added to actions that have rarely been tried, so the agent is drawn to them.
Q-learning with a function (e.g. a neural network) estimating the Q-values instead of a table.
deep Q-network: a neural network that takes a state and outputs one Q-value per action.
y = the reward observed + γ × the best Q-value predicted for the next state; what the network is trained towards.
a store of past (state, action, reward, next state, done, truncated) steps that training samples from at random.
a row of 0s with a 1 at the position of the action taken, used to keep only that action's Q-value.
the network suddenly losing what it had learned in one situation while learning another.
an activation like ReLU but with a smooth curve for negative inputs.
a copy of the network, updated only every so often, used to compute the targets so they hold still.
the network that learns at every step and chooses the agent's actions.
a DQN where the online model picks the next action and the target model says what it is worth.
taking the maximum of noisy estimates gives a number that is too high on average.
a DQN variant (a separate idea) that estimates a state's value and each action's advantage separately.
two networks: the actor (a policy) chooses actions, the critic estimates how good they are, so the actor improves after every step.
well-known actor-critic algorithms: A2C/A3C (advantage actor-critic), PPO (proximal policy optimization), SAC (soft actor-critic).
a classic arcade game used as a test for game-playing agents.
an ancient board game; DeepMind's AlphaGo beat the world champion at it in 2016.
arXiv is a free website where research papers are posted.
two harder gymnasium environments: land a craft on the moon; bounce a ball to break bricks (Atari).
a cheap credit-card-sized computer.
a version of TD learning that looks several steps ahead before updating.
replaying the stored experiences with the largest TD error more often.
the path the robot (or agent) actually follows, step by step.
with no chance involved: the same input always gives the same output (the opposite of stochastic).
a Python lookup table of name → value pairs; step()'s info is one.
a value that is either True or False.
an integer is a whole number (0, 1, 2); a float is a number with a decimal point (0.0274).
one still picture of the screen; a video or a game is a sequence of frames.
one dot of an image; its colour is stored as a number (or three: red, green, blue).
TensorFlow's name for an array of numbers with any number of dimensions (a list, a table, a table of tables…).
two meanings here. (1) A number each neuron adds to its weighted sum, learned like a weight. (2) In b11–b12: a systematic error, an estimate that is too high (or too low) on average.
settle on a final value and stop changing (much) as the steps go on.
the opposite of converge: the numbers grow without limit instead of settling.
how many numbers describe one thing (a four-dimensional observation is 4 numbers); in array code, one axis of the array (rows, columns).
a single number, not a list of numbers.
a group of examples used together for one update: in b06, the steps of 10 episodes; in b10, 32 stored steps picked at random.
synchronous = in step, everyone waits for everyone; asynchronous = each part goes ahead as soon as it is ready.
the graphics-card chip; it does thousands of small calculations at once, which makes neural networks much faster.
cut a value off at a limit, so it cannot go further than that limit.
right on average: not systematically too high or too low.
the gradient of the logarithm of the chosen action's probability: the direction that makes that action more likely.
square each error and average them; the loss b10 trains with.
learning from data that has no answer column, e.g. finding groups of similar rows.
a layer that slides small learned filters across an image to detect patterns such as edges; the standard layer for pictures.

preparing game frames before the network sees them: grayscale = black-and-white, cropped = edges cut off, downsampled = fewer pixels, stacked = several frames in a row given together so motion is visible.
ICML and AAAI are major AI research conferences and Nature is a leading science journal; papers they publish have been checked by other researchers.
a unit for angles: 1 radian ≈ 57.3°, so 0.036 radians ≈ 2°.
